blocks.heading: Start with the puzzle
blocks.text: A stock price is the present value of future payouts. A high price relative to current dividends can reflect strong expected dividend growth, low required future returns, or both. In postwar U.S. data, changes in required returns dominate this valuation variation. Earlier centuries look different. The paper asks why.

blocks.heading: The proposed mechanism
blocks.text: Firms paid out a smaller fraction of earnings after 1945. Retaining earnings pushes cash distributions farther into the future, increasing equity duration. Distant payouts are more exposed to persistent changes in discount rates. Expected returns are more persistent than expected dividend growth, and shocks to long-horizon expected returns can also be larger.

blocks.heading: A useful mental example
blocks.text: Imagine two claims on the same business: one pays only the next 18 months of dividends, while the other pays dividends indefinitely. A change in discount rates has more distant payments to affect in the second claim. This motivates the dividend-strip comparison without requiring different firms.

blocks.heading: What the evidence does and does not establish
blocks.text: The paper triangulates across dividend strips, four centuries of aggregate market data, and payout-sorted portfolios. The consistency supports the duration interpretation. Payout is a proxy for duration, however, and the empirical comparisons alone do not establish a randomized causal effect. Section 4 adds a calibrated model, which your assignment excludes.

blocks.heading: Reading route
blocks.text: Read the introduction (pp. 1-2), equations (9)-(11) and Table 1 (p. 4), Table 2 (p. 5), data construction (pp. 6-7), Figure 1 and Table 5 (pp. 8-9), and Tables 6-7 plus Figure 3 (pp. 10-11). Finish with the qualifications and conclusion (pp. 12-13).

blocks.heading: Keep three quantities distinct
blocks.text: Payout is dividends divided by earnings: it proxies for how much a firm distributes now. The dividend-to-price ratio is dividends divided by market price: it is the forecasting variable. Duration measures the timing of distributions. These concepts are related, but are not interchangeable.

blocks.heading: Forecasting regressions
blocks.text: For the market, regress next-period real log returns, real log dividend growth, and the next log dividend-to-price ratio separately on the current log dividend-to-price ratio, including an intercept. Call the slopes b_ret, b_dg, and b_dp. Match the paper's horizon and observation frequency before comparing coefficients.

blocks.heading: Decomposition
blocks.text: Equation (10): ER = b_ret / (1 - rho*b_dp); EDG = -b_dg / (1 - rho*b_dp). Here rho is the log-linearization parameter, based on the average log dividend-to-price ratio; it is not simply the sample autocorrelation. ER measures the expected-return contribution to variation in the log dividend-to-price ratio; EDG measures the expected-dividend-growth contribution. These are not regression R-squared values.

blocks.heading: Approximation and implied values
blocks.text: The present-value approximation implies ER + EDG is about one. Estimated direct shares need not sum to exactly one. Implied ER is 1 - EDG; implied EDG is 1 - ER. A negative share or ER above one can occur in finite-sample estimates; do not clip it to make a probability.

blocks.heading: Dividend strips and inference
blocks.text: For the finite dividend-strip claim, the paper uses ER = b_ret and EDG = -b_dg. Table 2 uses monthly observations with overlapping 12-month outcomes and Newey-West standard errors with 12 lags, plus average t-statistics across 12 non-overlapping subsamples. Tables 5 and 7 use annual observations and one Newey-West lag. Preserve the sign of EDG and each table's units.

title: Evidence block 1: strips versus the market

blocks.heading: Assigned exhibits: Tables 1 and 2
blocks.text: Table 1 (p. 4) describes real 12-month returns, dividend growth and dividend-to-price ratios for January 1996-December 2022. Table 2 (p. 5) compares predictability for the S&P 500 market claim with short-duration claims on its dividends.

blocks.heading: What to notice
blocks.text: In Table 2 the direct ER estimate is 0.96 for the market versus 0.56 for strips. The corresponding EDG estimates are 0.05 and 0.40. These are published benchmarks, not results generated by this repository. The contrast is consistent with expected returns explaining more valuation variation for the longer-duration claim.

blocks.heading: Construction details
blocks.text: The strip-return strategy uses maturities around 1.3-1.9 years and rebalances every January and July. The strip predictor uses an 18-month constant-maturity price and trailing 12-month S&P dividends. Do not casually equate the strategy maturity with the predictor maturity. Outcomes and dividends must use compatible inflation adjustments.

blocks.heading: Data and validation plan
blocks.text: Start with the authors' Mendeley package and Benjamin Golez's dividend-strip series. The paper uses Datastream for S&P prices and total returns; the course permits CRSP as a substitute. Record differences in coverage and conventions. Check calendar joins, duplicate months, price positivity, inflation units, missing outcomes, and return/dividend reconstruction against author series.

blocks.heading: Main caveat
blocks.text: Strip prices inferred from option put-call matches can contain measurement error, biasing ER upward. The paper studies lagged moving-average predictors in Table 3. Table 3 is not assigned, but its discussion is useful for interpreting Table 2. Do not treat short-horizon strip estimates as noise-free measurements.

title: Evidence block 2: four centuries of history

blocks.heading: Assigned exhibits: Tables 4 and 5; Figure 1
blocks.text: Table 4 (p. 7) summarizes annual real variables. Figure 1 (p. 8) plots payout and dividend-to-price ratios. Table 5 (p. 9) compares historical predictability. The published Table 5 has postwar, prewar and full-sample columns, not four separate historical subperiod columns.

blocks.heading: Sample geography matters
blocks.text: The long series combines Netherlands/U.K. markets for 1629-1812, the U.K. for 1813-1870, and the U.S. from 1871 onward. It is not a continuous U.S. series. Earnings coverage is more limited than price/dividend coverage; do not fill missing early earnings with zeros. Before 1700 the paper uses trailing dividend smoothing for some measures.

blocks.heading: What to notice
blocks.text: Table 5 reports direct ER of 0.91 for 1945-2022, 0.34 for 1629-1945 and 0.40 for the full sample. EDG is 0.10, 0.63 and 0.55. Table 4 reports payout of 47.26% postwar versus 98.41% prewar, with a coverage qualification on the latter. These are published reference values.

blocks.heading: Figure 1 is easy to misread
blocks.text: Panel A uses dividends over earnings aggregated over a trailing 10-year window. Panel B averages annual dividend-to-price ratios over a trailing 10-year window. A ratio of sums is not the mean of annual ratios. Despite the title Total payout, the baseline analysis focuses on cash dividends, not a generic dividends-plus-buybacks series.

blocks.heading: Replication decisions to freeze
blocks.text: Match rolling-window endpoints, inflation adjustments, log versus level measures, annual return timing, and the 1945 boundary using the authors' code. The Figure 1 caption has an inconsistent 2017 endpoint in one sentence; the title and plot run through 2022. Ask the instructor about the version discrepancies before changing exhibit definitions.

blocks.heading: Assigned exhibits: Tables 6 and 7; Figure 3
blocks.text: Table 6 (p. 10) summarizes portfolio composition and annual variables; Table 7 on the same page estimates predictability. Figure 3 (p. 11) combines the historical and cross-sectional evidence in a plot of ER versus payout. Recreating only the portfolio dots would omit part of Figure 3.

blocks.heading: Build a point-in-time stock panel
blocks.text: Use common stocks with CRSP share codes 10 and 11, monthly returns and dividends, and Compustat net income. Before 1950 the paper uses clean-surplus earnings with Davis-Fama-French book equity: earnings = change in book equity + repurchases - issuance + dividends. Verify identifiers, linking dates, delistings, splits and units against the replication code.

blocks.heading: Sort using only the past
blocks.text: The paper requires non-missing earnings and nonzero dividends over the preceding 10 years. Its example forms the 1946 portfolios from 1936-1945 information. Rebalance annually and value-weight using market capitalization. Create low, medium and high payout terciles, plus below/above 0.5 portfolios and the all-stocks benchmark.

blocks.heading: Exceptional observations
blocks.text: Negative trailing payout is treated as high payout and set to the 99th percentile according to the paper. When computing the dividend-smoothing parameter, years with negative earnings in any portfolio are removed for all portfolios. Read the authors' code to settle quantile conventions and timing; do not choose them to fit the answer.

blocks.heading: What to notice and test
blocks.text: Table 7 direct ER falls from 1.04 in the low-payout tercile to 0.54 in the high-payout tercile. Test that formation inputs predate holding returns, portfolio weights sum to one, buckets cover eligible firms without overlap within each sorting scheme, and filter counts reconcile. Maintain an explicit common sample for comparisons.

title: From replication to a useful product

blocks.heading: Build in stages
blocks.text: 1. Freeze source versions and the eight exhibit definitions. 2. Fetch and inventory the authors' package. 3. Implement ingestion and cleaning separately from estimation. 4. Replicate original-sample outputs and compare against predetermined tolerances. 5. Extend each dataset to its latest available date. 6. Deliver the instructor-approved extension and a clean-clone pipeline.

blocks.heading: Candidate extension, not yet agreed
blocks.text: An equity-duration research monitor could let an empirical-finance researcher compare ER/EDG across trailing windows and payout groups, inspect uncertainty and sample coverage, and download documented permitted derived outputs. Its value would be sensitivity analysis and transparent source lineage, beyond merely refreshing the endpoint.

blocks.heading: One-page consultation pitch
blocks.text: Claim: payout-related duration helps explain the postwar rise in ER. Gap: researchers need to see how sensitive that relation is to windows, data vintages and portfolio screens. Build: a reproducible monitor with a baseline and prespecified robustness controls. User: asset-pricing researchers auditing valuation decompositions. Success: baseline replication within frozen tolerances, transparent coverage, and independently tested changes under each control.

blocks.heading: Validation and rubric checklist
blocks.text: Distinguish numerical replication tests from data-validation tests. Plan source reconciliation, accounting/return identities, portfolio weights, filter attrition and temporal coverage checks. Produce at least one original validation table and figure. Register completed dataframes/charts and their sources in chartbook.toml. The final report must be LaTeX with generated statistics, and the final site needs a notebook touring cleaned data.
